lines.text: A land of great rivers and the Bay of Bengal, of poets, monsoons and a hard-won freedom. This is the story of Bangladesh.
In the eighth century the Pala kings of Bengal built a Buddhist empire that ruled much of north India for four hundred years.
They raised Somapura Mahavihara, one of the largest Buddhist monasteries south of the Himalayas, whose ruins still stand in the north of the country.
In 1352 Bengal became a rich Muslim kingdom of its own, the Bengal Sultanate, famous for its trade and its mosques.
In 1608 the Mughals made Dhaka the capital of Bengal. Known then for its fine muslin, it is today one of the most crowded cities on Earth.
In 1757, at Plassey, Robert Clive and the East India Company defeated the Nawab of Bengal through betrayal. British rule in India began here.
In 1861 Rabindranath Tagore was born, the Bengali poet who won the Nobel Prize and wrote the song that became the anthem of Bangladesh.
Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, born in 1920, would lead the struggle for independence and be honoured as the father of the nation.
Ziaur Rahman, an army officer, would declare independence over the radio in 1971, and later rule the country until he was killed.
Muhammad Yunus, born in 1940, would lend tiny sums to the poor, win the Nobel Peace Prize, and one day lead his country.
In 1943, in the middle of the Second World War, famine struck Bengal. Crop disease, wartime chaos and failed policy cost millions of lives.
Khaleda Zia, born in 1945, would become the country's first woman prime minister.
Two years later came her great rival, Sheikh Hasina, Mujib's daughter, who would lead the country for twenty years in all.
After partition, the east of Bengal became part of Pakistan. When Urdu was pressed on them, students in Dhaka died in 1952 defending their Bengali tongue.
In 1970 the Bhola cyclone struck the low coast, one of the deadliest storms ever recorded. Anger at the slow relief from the west fed the call for freedom.
In 1971 a new nation declared itself: Bangladesh, the land of the Bengalis.
It won its independence from Pakistan only after a terrible war that year, with India at its side by the end.
From the late seventies, clothing factories began to spring up, until Bangladesh became the second-largest exporter of clothes in the world.
In 1983 Muhammad Yunus founded the Grameen Bank, giving small loans to the poor, most of them women, with no need for property.
In 1991 another cyclone came in from the Bay of Bengal and killed about a hundred and forty thousand people.
In 1999 the United Nations made the twenty-first of February International Mother Language Day, in honour of the students of 1952.
In 2013 the Rana Plaza factory building collapsed near Dhaka after workers were sent back in despite cracks, the deadliest disaster the garment trade has known.
In 2022 the Padma Bridge opened, carrying road and rail over the great river, the largest building project in the nation's history.
And in the summer of 2024, a student uprising forced Sheikh Hasina to flee, and a new chapter began.
From the Palas to the students of 2024, Bangladesh has always been shaped by its people and its rivers.
